entry: Measure of distance in physical space. Length is commonly understood as the most extended dimension of a fixed object, though this depends on the object's position. Most systems of measurement choose a base unit for length from which all other units are derived; in the [[International System of Units|International System of Units (SI)]] it is the [[Metre|meter]]. Length measures one spatial dimension, whereas [[Area|area]] measures two (length squared) and [[Volume|volume]] three (length cubed). Under [[Special relativity|special relativity]], length is not constant across reference frames: a ruler one meter long in one frame is not one meter long in a frame moving relative to it. In Euclidean geometry, length is measured along straight lines, and the perimeter of a [[Polygon|polygon]] is the sum of its side lengths.

German filmmaker, photographer and actress. Riefenstahl began as a dancer and actress, starring in five films between 1925 and 1929, and directed her first film, *The Blue Light*, in 1932. She then made two [[Propaganda|propaganda]] films for the Nazi regime: *Triumph of the Will* (1935), which chronicled the 1934 Nuremberg Rally, and *Olympia* (1938), on the 1936 Berlin Games. Both are widely considered two of the most effective and technically innovative propaganda films ever made. [[Adolf Hitler|Hitler]] collaborated closely with her on at least three Nazi films. After [[World War II]], she was arrested and classified as a Nazi "fellow traveler" but was not charged with [[War crime|war crimes]]. She denied having known about the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]]. Her postwar work included the film *Tiefland* (released 1954), underwater photography and photo books on the Nuba peoples of southern Sudan.

American singer, songwriter and record producer. His debut album, *Let Love Rule* (1989), blended rock, funk, reggae and soul. Hits include "Are You Gonna Go My Way" (1993) and "Again" (2000). He won four consecutive [[Grammy Awards]] for Best Male Rock Vocal Performance, from 1999 to 2002, and has sold over 40 million albums worldwide. Kravitz also acted in *Precious* (2009) and the first two *Hunger Games* films.

Hong Kong-based Chinese multinational technology company. Lenovo makes [[Personal computer|personal computers]], [[Smartphone|smartphones]], servers and [[Data storage|data storage]] devices. Originally known as Legend, a distributor of foreign IT products, it merged with IBM's PC business in 2005, gaining the ThinkPad line. In 2013 it became the world's largest personal computer vendor by unit sales for the first time, a position it still held as of 2024. Its global headquarters are in [[Beijing]] and Morrisville, [[North Carolina]], in the [[United States]].

Type of galaxy intermediate between [[Elliptical galaxy|elliptical]] and [[Spiral galaxy|spiral]] galaxies, denoted S0. It has a large-scale disk but no large-scale spiral arms. Lenticular galaxies have used up or lost most of their [[Interstellar medium|interstellar matter]], so they have very little ongoing [[Star formation|star formation]] and consist mainly of aging stars, though they may retain significant dust in their disks. Their featureless disk does not fit the spiral classes, and their spherical bulge does not fit the elliptical ones, so they are subdivided by dust content (S01 to S03) or by a central bar (SB01 to SB03). Lenticular and elliptical galaxies share spectral features and scaling relations, and both are considered passively evolving early-type galaxies in the local universe. They are often viewed as a poorly understood transition state between spiral and elliptical galaxies in [[Galaxy morphological classification|morphological classification]].

Annual [[Legume|legume]] grown for its lens-shaped edible seeds, also called lentils. The bushy plant normally grows 30 to 50 centimeters tall, and each pod usually holds two seeds. Lentils originated in the Near East and were domesticated in the [[Fertile Crescent]], spreading to Europe, Egypt and the [[Indian subcontinent]]. The seeds are used worldwide, most commonly in [[Stew|stews]] and [[Soup|soups]]; split lentils, known as dal, are cooked into a thick curry eaten with rice or roti. One cup of cooked lentils (198 g) provides 18 g of protein and 16 g of fiber. As a rotational crop, lentils fix 30–100 pounds of nitrogen per acre. Major producers include [[Australia]], Canada, India, [[Turkey]] and the United States.

Belgian-born American chemist and inventor. Educated in Belgium and Germany, he taught physics and chemistry in [[Bruges]] and then at [[Ghent]] University. In 1889 he visited the United States, where [[Columbia University]] professor Charles F. Chandler persuaded him to stay. He developed Velox, the first commercially successful photographic paper, and founded the Nepera Chemical Company, which he sold to George Eastman of Kodak in 1899 for $750,000. In 1907 he invented [[Bakelite]], a durable, heat-resistant [[Plastic|plastic]] made by combining [[Phenol|phenol]] and [[Formaldehyde|formaldehyde]]. He has been called "The Father of the Plastics Industry" for the invention, which marked the beginning of the modern plastics industry.

Byzantine emperor, 717–741, and founder of the Isaurian dynasty. Originally named Konon, he was born in Germanikeia, near the northern border of Syria, and commanded the Anatolic theme in [[Anatolia]] before seizing the throne in 717. He was crowned at [[Hagia Sophia]]. He ended the Twenty Years' Anarchy, a period of rapid imperial succession between 695 and 717. In August 717 the second Arab siege of Constantinople began, and he withstood it partly through the use of [[Greek fire]]. He successfully defended the empire against the [[Umayyad Caliphate|Umayyads]] and forbade the veneration of icons, initiating [[Iconoclasm|Byzantine Iconoclasm]] in 726–730. Most modern scholars reject the nickname "the Isaurian" as a misnomer, since Leo came from Syria rather than Isauria.

Italian Renaissance [[Humanism|humanist]] and [[Polymath|polymath]]. Alberti was an author, artist, architect, poet, priest, linguist, philosopher and cryptographer, and he is considered the founder of European [[Cryptography|cryptography]]. He wrote *Della pittura* (1435), an early treatise on painting that analyzed [[Perspective (graphical)|perspective]], composition and color. His architectural works include the Palazzo Rucellai (begun 1446) and the upper part of the façade of Santa Maria Novella, both in [[Florence]], and the Tempio Malatestiano in Rimini. In 1452 he completed *De re aedificatoria*, a treatise on architecture based on the work of [[Vitruvius]], though it was not published until 1485. In Mantua he designed the Basilica of Sant'Andrea, which was completed after his death and is considered his most significant work. [[Giorgio Vasari|Giorgio Vasari]] wrote about his life in *Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects*.

American [[Social psychology|social psychologist]]. Festinger originated the theory of [[Cognitive dissonance|cognitive dissonance]] and social comparison theory, and his research helped displace the behaviorist view of social psychology. He studied under [[Kurt Lewin]] at the University of Iowa, and in 1945 he joined Lewin's Research Center for Group Dynamics at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] as a faculty member. He advanced the use of laboratory experiments in social psychology while stressing the importance of real-life situations, and he personally infiltrated a doomsday cult to study it. He is also known in [[Social network|social network]] theory for the proximity effect. Later he turned to visual perception and then to archaeology, history and the human evolutionary sciences. He was the fifth most cited psychologist of the 20th century, after B. F. Skinner, Jean Piaget, Sigmund Freud and Albert Bandura.

Russian revolutionary and Soviet politician. Trotsky helped lead the [[October Revolution]] of 1917. As People's Commissar for Foreign Affairs he negotiated the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, by which Russia withdrew from [[World War I]]. As People's Commissar for Military Affairs from 1918 to 1925 he built the [[Red Army]] and led it to victory in the [[Russian Civil War]]. After Lenin's death, he was outmaneuvered by [[Joseph Stalin]], expelled from the party in 1927 and deported from the [[Soviet Union]] in 1929. In exile he argued that the Soviet Union had become a "degenerated workers' state," and in 1938 he founded the Fourth International. He was assassinated in Mexico City by a Stalinist agent. Scholarship ranks his leadership of the Red Army highly, while critics point to his ideological defense of the Red Terror and the suppression of the Kronstadt rebellion.

American conductor, composer and pianist. He was the first American-born conductor to receive international acclaim and was music director of the New York Philharmonic from 1958 to 1969. His works include the Broadway musical *West Side Story* (1957), which retells *Romeo and Juliet* in a modern urban setting, the theater work *Candide* (1956) and the score for Elia Kazan's *On the Waterfront* (1954). He hosted the New York Philharmonic's *Young People's Concerts* from 1958 to 1972, bringing classical music to a mass television audience. He was also a critical figure in the modern revival of the music of [[Gustav Mahler]]. In 1970 he held a fundraiser for the legal defense of the [[Black Panther Party]], which drew criticism as elite liberal posturing; satirist Tom Wolfe later termed it "radical chic." On Christmas Day 1989 he conducted Beethoven's *Symphony No. 9* in Berlin to celebrate the [[Fall of the Berlin Wall|fall of the Berlin Wall]].

Canadian singer-songwriter, poet and novelist. Cohen published poetry and novels in the 1950s and early 1960s before beginning a music career in 1966. His work explores faith and mortality, betrayal and redemption, and sexual and romantic love. His most famous song, "[[Hallelujah (Leonard Cohen song)|Hallelujah]]," appeared on *Various Positions* (1984). He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] and invested as a Companion of the Order of Canada. *You Want It Darker* (2016) was released three weeks before his death.

American actor, director, photographer and author. Nimoy is famous for playing [[Spock]] in the [[Star Trek]] franchise, a role he originated in the original series in 1966. He directed *Star Trek III: The Search for Spock* (1984) and *Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home* (1986), and he starred in *Mission: Impossible* for two seasons. He died of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and an [[Asteroid|asteroid]] was named 4864 Nimoy in his honor.

American actor and film producer. DiCaprio achieved international fame with *Titanic* (1997) and won the Academy Award for Best Actor for *The Revenant* (2015). He frequently worked with director [[Martin Scorsese]], beginning with *Gangs of New York* (2002). Other films include *Inception* (2010), *The Wolf of Wall Street* (2013) and *Killers of the Flower Moon* (2023). He is a United Nations Messenger of Peace and founded the Leonardo DiCaprio Foundation, a nonprofit devoted to promoting environmental awareness.

Soviet politician and General Secretary of the [[Communist Party of the Soviet Union]] from 1964 to 1982. He also served as [[Head of state|head of state]] from 1960 to 1964 and again from 1977 to 1982. Brezhnev took part in removing [[Nikita Khrushchev]] in 1964, shared power in a collective leadership, and by the end of the 1960s had become the dominant figure in the Soviet leadership. He pursued détente with the [[United States]] while achieving nuclear parity, and military interventions expanded Soviet influence in the Middle East and Africa. The 1968 Warsaw Pact invasion of [[Czechoslovakia]] enforced the Brezhnev Doctrine of limited sovereignty over socialist states. His rule saw increased repression and censorship, and an era of stagnation marked by shrinking consumer goods and declining growth. [[Mikhail Gorbachev]] later denounced his government for inefficiency, yet polls in post-Soviet Russia have shown consistently high approval of his rule.

King of [[Sparta]] and member of the Agiad dynasty, c. 489–480 BC. He succeeded his half-brother Cleomenes I and ruled jointly with Leotychidas II. Leonidas led the allied Greek forces at the [[Battle of Thermopylae]] against the Persian army of [[Xerxes I]] during the Second Persian War. He was killed early on the third and last day of the battle. Leonidas entered myth as a hero and the leader of the 300 Spartans who died with him. Although the Greeks lost the battle, they expelled the Persians the following year at the Battle of Plataea. [[Plutarch]] recorded his reply to a critic: "But were I not better than you, I should not be king."

Spotted cat in the genus [[Panthera]], native to Africa and Asia. The leopard, *Panthera pardus*, has pale yellowish to dark golden fur with dark spots grouped in rosettes, a pattern that aids [[Camouflage|camouflage]] as it stalks prey. Males typically weigh 30.9–72 kg, and females 20.5–43 kg. [[Carl Linnaeus]] first described it in 1758, and eight subspecies are recognized today. It adapts to habitats from [[Rainforest|rainforest]] to [[Steppe|steppe]]. It is an opportunistic predator, mostly hunting hooved mammals and primates, and it often drags its kills up a tree. Females usually bear a litter of 2–4 cubs once in 15–24 months. Listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, leopards face habitat loss and fragmentation.

Antarctic seal, the only species in the genus *Hydrurga*. It is the second largest seal in the Antarctic after the southern elephant seal, and it is the same length as but half the weight of a walrus. Its countershaded coat is silver below and dark gray above, with leopard-like dark spots. As an [[Apex predator|apex predator]] with massive jaws, it eats [[Krill|krill]], fish, [[Cephalopod|cephalopods]], other [[Pinniped|pinnipeds]] and [[Penguin|penguins]]. Its only natural predator is the [[Orca|orca]], and it uses its hearing and [[Whiskers|whiskers]] to track prey underwater.

King of the Belgians, 1865–1909, and sole owner of the [[Congo Free State]]. Leopold was born in [[Brussels]] and is popularly called the Builder King in Belgium for the buildings, urban projects and public works he commissioned. He reigned for 44 years. As founder of the Congo Free State, a private colonial project, he never visited the territory and ran it through the mercenary Force Publique. He extracted a fortune first from [[Ivory|ivory]] and then, after rubber prices rose in the 1890s, from rubber harvested by forced labor. His administration was marked by systematic brutality, including the amputation of hands and sometimes feet when rubber quotas were not met. Estimates of the population decline under his rule range from 1 million to 15 million. Under international pressure, Belgium annexed the territory as the Belgian Congo in 1908.

Holy Roman Emperor, 1658–1705, and king of Hungary, Croatia and Bohemia. The second son of Ferdinand III, Leopold was a composer and a considerable patron of music. He was educated in the liberal arts and natural science, and he was knowledgeable about theology. A devout Catholic, he personified the *pietas Austriaca*, and he retained an interest in [[Astrology|astrology]] from his Jesuit education. He fought the [[Ottoman Empire|Ottomans]] in the Great Turkish War (1683–1699). Forces under [[John III Sobieski]] relieved [[Vienna]] in 1683, and the military talents of [[Prince Eugene of Savoy]] brought victory. The Treaty of Karlowitz recovered almost all of the [[Kingdom of Hungary]]. He fought three wars against [[Louis XIV]]'s France, the last being the [[War of the Spanish Succession]], which he started to secure the Spanish inheritance for his younger son. That war lasted until 1714.

German historian and a founder of modern source-based history. Ranke set standards for much of later historical writing. He introduced reliance on primary sources ([[Empiricism|empiricism]]) and emphasized narrative history, especially international politics. His 1824 work *Histories of the Latin and Teutonic Peoples* drew on memoirs, diaries, government documents and eyewitness accounts. From 1825 he taught at the University of [[Berlin]] for nearly fifty years, where he established the first historical seminar and taught students to check the value of sources. He criticized the [[Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel|Hegelian]] view of history as a one-size-fits-all approach. Ranke was ennobled in 1865, adding "von" to his name. Critics note that his Lutheran belief that [[God]]'s actions were manifest in history shaped his view that the [[German Empire]] was a manifestation of God's intent.

Order of winged [[Insect|insects]] including [[Butterfly|butterflies]] and [[Moth|moths]]. The name comes from the [[Ancient Greek]] words for "scale" and "wing," reflecting the colored scales that cover their bodies. Almost all species have membranous wings and a proboscis for drinking nectar. Butterflies and moths undergo complete [[Metamorphosis|metamorphosis]], passing through a [[Larva|larval]] caterpillar stage, a pupa and an adult. Caterpillars are mostly herbivorous and can be [[Agriculture|agricultural]] pests, while adults feed on nectar and serve as economically useful [[Pollination|pollinators]]. About 180,000 species have been described, making Lepidoptera the second largest insect order after beetles. Lepidopterans first appeared in the fossil record at the Triassic–Jurassic boundary, and they have coevolved with flowering plants since the Cretaceous. Females often produce up to 600 eggs.

Diminutive [[Supernatural|supernatural]] being in [[Ireland|Irish]] folklore. Leprechauns are usually depicted as little bearded men in a coat and hat who play mischief. Some classify them as a solitary [[Fairy|fairy]] whose principal occupation is making and cobbling shoes. Leprechaun-like creatures rarely appear in Irish mythology and became prominent only in later folklore. The earliest known reference is in the medieval tale *Echtra Fergus mac Léti*, in which King Fergus of [[Ulster]], dragged toward the sea by three leprechauns, captures them and wins three wishes in exchange for their release. In later times they were depicted as shoemakers guarding a hidden pot of gold at the end of the [[Rainbow|rainbow]]. One etymology combines roots meaning "small" and "body," but 2019 research links the word to the Roman Luperci and the festival of Lupercalia.

Chronic infectious disease, also called Hansen's disease, caused by the [[Bacteria|bacterium]] *Mycobacterium leprae*. Infection damages nerves, skin, eyes and the upper respiratory tract. Nerve damage can cause loss of pain sensation, leading to unnoticed injuries and the loss of parts of the extremities. Symptoms may begin within a year or take 20 years or more to appear. Transmission requires extensive contact, and about 95% of people exposed to the bacterium do not develop the disease. It is curable with multidrug therapy, which the [[World Health Organization]] provides free of charge. India, Brazil and [[Indonesia]] account for over 80% of cases, and new detections fell to 172,717 in 2024 from 182,815 in 2023. Separating patients in leper colonies is not supported by evidence, but the practice still occurred in some areas as of the late 2000s.
